body: He has been up since midnight, as he was told, sitting on the edge of his bed in the back bedroom with the lamp off and the RAZR open in his hand, so that the little screen lights and goes out and lights again whenever his thumb moves. Across from him the parka is folded on Danny’s bed.

He puts the Carhartt on over his pajama pants and goes down in his socks. At the seventh stair he steps long, to the eighth, and the house never hears him. The tree is lit in the front room for Nonna, who is asleep in her chair under it with her rosary gone slack in her lap. He goes past her and through the kitchen without a light, and opens the basement door, and pulls it to behind him.

There’s no window down here worth the name, and he doesn’t pull the string on the bulb. He knows the basement in the dark: the Dell dark on its card table, Ma’s laundry baskets, the laundry sink empty. He doesn’t sit on the steps. He crosses the concrete and sits down on the floor with his back against the furnace, against the warm sheet-metal flank of it, and the heat comes through the Carhartt into his shoulders while the floor sends its chill up through the flannel of his pajama pants to meet it. The furnace is running. He can feel it in his spine.
At 1:34 the phone goes off in his hand, and he has it open before the first buzz is done.
“Hey.”

“Hi.” Her voice is low and close, with something soft over it — a blanket, from the sound. “I’m in my childhood bed. It’s a twin. There’s a corkboard over it with every call sheet from the year I was twelve, and the print ad from the hamburger thing, so I’m being watched by me in a paper hat. My mother is at a network thing in Burbank until God knows. The parrot’s asleep under a towel. I have the entire apartment to myself and I’m lying in the bed I had braces in.” The springs go: she has turned over, or settled. “You owe me a five-day.”
“There’s no window down here.”
“Did I ask about a window? You’ve lived there your entire life. Do it from memory.” A rustle. “And use your hand. I can hear it when you don’t use your hand.”
He puts his free hand out into the dark toward the Dell, where a map would be.
“Tuesday,” he says. “Cold. Gray all day, a high just under freezing, flurries off the lake by noon. Salt trucks on Market Street by two.”
“Better. Wednesday.”
“Colder.”
“Colder isn’t a forecast. Colder is a mood.”
“Wednesday, a lot colder. Car doors frozen shut. My father out in the driveway with a kettle.”
“Thursday.”
“A full moon. Second one this month, so it’s a blue moon.”
“Is it blue?”
“No. It’s just extra.”
“That’s not weather, Jack. That’s astronomy.”
“Ask anybody with a boat.”
“Friday.”
“Friday’s yours. The Rose Bowl. Pasadena, sunny and seventy, Ohio State and Oregon, and every man on Glenwood Avenue yelling at a quarterback in California who can’t hear him.”
“Seventy is generous. Saturday.”
“Saturday, flurries. The tree stays up. My grandmother says it comes down after the Epiphany, and in this house what she says about a tree is final.”
“You did the hand for Wednesday and then you quit on the hand.”
“You can’t see my hand.”
“I can *hear* it,” Skye says. “Seven. The moon carried you.”
Under the blanket in Studio City a page turns. He knows that sound; he’d know it in his sleep.

“I have forty pages left,” she says, “and I’m not reading them, because then he stops talking. Your guy’s a dancer. He does the entire book on one foot and never falls over. It’s infuriating. Every time I think I’ve caught him at something he’s already in the next room, eating.”
“He’d like that you said that.”

“He’d make a joke about my weight.” Another page. “The fairy-tale chapter. The palace — gold, sapphire, the works. You get to live in it forever, and the one condition is there’s a word you can’t say. And out of every word in English, Jack. Out of every single one. He picked *cow*.”
“It’s a good word.”

“It’s the *perfect* word. It’s the funniest word in the language and he knew it, and he put it in the middle of the most beautiful thing in the book like a whoopee cushion on a throne.” The blanket moves. When she goes on, she’s lower. “Here’s what he gets wrong, though. He thinks the condition is the price. You pay it, you keep the palace. But you don’t even want the palace till somebody tells you there’s a word you can’t say. The no is what makes you want it.”
He turns that over against the warm metal, with the floor coming up through him.
“It’s the shape of the gift,” he says. “The condition. A palace has doors. That’s part of it being a palace.”
“You’re describing me,” Skye says.
He doesn’t have an answer to that which isn’t her name.

body.text: “And you owe me a *who*,” she says. “Saturday it was a promise. A promise to *who*. I said Monday. It’s Monday.”
“To whoever gave her the dress,” he says. “The one who wants her home.”
“So she isn’t running back to the prince.”
“The prince is the one who goes out looking.”
The mattress gives. “That’s a whole theology,” Skye says, “and you did it with a shoe.”
“Did you open my tree?” she says.
“Good.” Her breath, close to the phone. “…Open it now.”
“Did you keep my tree?” she says.
The blanket moves on her end. “…Good. The lighting was bad.”

body: “So,” Skye says. “No questions tonight. I’m not going to ask you one thing. No cow.”
The bed takes her weight differently; he hears her settle into it, the springs and then nothing.
“Monday,” Skye says. “Not asking. Telling.”

choices.key: The Monday after Christmas Skye called and stopped asking. You told her to tell you.
response: “Then tell me.”
A breath on her end, close to the phone. She begins.

choices.key: The Monday after Christmas Skye called and stopped asking. You told her it was already Tuesday in Ohio.
response: “It’s Tuesday here.”
“Then you’re late,” Skye says. “You’re three hours late, Costigan, and I’ve been lying here the entire time getting ready.”
She begins.

choices.key: The Monday after Christmas Skye called and stopped asking. You said nothing, and let her start.
response: He doesn’t say anything.
Behind him the furnace goes on with its work. On her end the bed creaks and goes still, and she waits out his nothing, and then she starts.

choices.text: *Open the one you saved. Now, while she’s on the line.*
choices.key: The Monday after Christmas Skye called and stopped asking. You opened the picture you’d saved since Christmas Eve while she was on the line.
response: “Hang on.”
“Oh, I’m not going anywhere,” Skye says.

He takes the phone down from his ear. In the inbox the envelope from Christmas Eve is still sitting where he left it, and he opens it. *Retrieving.* The screen is the only light in the basement, and the picture comes down it in bands, slow, top to bottom, so he gets the tree before he gets her: white, flocked so thick it looks frosted by hand, and a wedge of carpet, and at the edge of the frame a green parrot on a perch with its head turned, deeply put out. Then her hair, fanned on the carpet in the tree’s shadow. Then her.

She took it lying on her back under the tree with her arm straight up, aiming down at herself without looking, so the camera hangs over her at the height of somebody kneeling there — and the somebody, now, holding the phone in a basement in his socks, is him. One strand of the tree’s small white lights is wound loose around her, over a shoulder and across and around a hip, and it is all she has on. Each bulb makes a warm coin of light on her skin, and the rest of her belongs to the brown dusk of a living room at four in the afternoon. She has her lip pinned under her teeth against a laugh, and her eyes are right on the lens.
He holds it at his knee in the dark and looks.
When he gets the phone back to his ear she says, “I can hear you looking.” And then, softer: “There he is.”
She begins.

body: Where comes first, and it comes in a voice, singsong and pleased with itself, a babysitter’s voice for a kid who won’t go down: “Once upon a time,” Skye says, “in a little room in Studio City, under a corkboard, on a twin bed —” and stops herself. “No. God, no. Not here. My mother would *know*. She’d know from the carpet.” The blanket moves. “The Saab. The turnout by the Marine Lab, top up, engine off, and the windows gone white, so there’s no ocean and no road and no anybody. Just the inside of my car. That’s where.” The springs. “And it’s the night you don’t say no. I’m not asking which night. I’m telling you what happens on it.”

“You come down past the chain in that coat, and you knock on my window like it’s a front door and somebody’s mother might answer. I lean across and open it. You get in. You’re cold, and you smell like that coat, and you don’t get to say anything; you used up all your talking in December. I take the coat first.”

She tells him the order. The Carhartt, off his shoulders and down his arms, and she’ll keep his arms caught in the sleeves longer than he likes, on purpose. His shirt next, up over his head, slow, so it catches on his ears and he has to sit there in the dark with his arms up and his face in it while she looks at him. Then she tells him what stays.

“The medal stays. I’m leaving it on you.” Her voice has come down under the blanket with her. “I’ve thought about that more than I should. How cold it is when it touches me first. How it goes warm if you wait.”
Under his T-shirt his own medal lies against his breastbone, where it has lain since his confirmation. He hasn’t thought about it in days. He can feel exactly where it is now.

“And you’re doing the clasp. I’m not helping. I’m going to lie back against the door with my arms up and let you lose to it for as long as it takes.” There’ll be static, she says. There is always static in that car. It’ll be in her hair, and when her hair comes down over him it’ll crackle, and she wants him to hear it.
“I’m keeping the anklet. That’s all I’m keeping. Everything else is yours to deal with.”

“Also I’m going to hit my knee on the gearshift. I want that known now. I hit it every single time, and I’m going to hit it then, and I’m going to swear, and you’re going to laugh at me, and I’m going to let you, once.” He laughs now, on the floor, with no sound, and on her end he hears her hear it.

Behind him the furnace shuts off. In the quiet he can hear his own breathing, and hers, and under hers the springs of a twin bed in Studio City when somebody turns over on it. He’s hard. He has been since she said *the turnout*, and there is nothing on a basement floor to be done about that, and nobody to hide it from but the furnace.
Here is where he could stop her.

He doesn’t. He can’t say yes. He has never been able to say yes to her — not on her floor, not in the Saab with the windows white, not on the bluff with no moon — and he can’t say it tonight, and under all of it he knows he won’t be able to say it in January either. So he doesn’t stop her. He lets it go on, and on, because this is the only yes there is.
“I’m going to say your name,” Skye says. “Not all of it. Just Jack. Once when I’ve got you down to the medal, like I’m checking it’s really you. And once after that. You’ll know when.”

She tells him what else she’ll say, and when. *Slower*, when he isn’t. *Look at me*, when he doesn’t. *Eyes open*, when he starts to close them. And at the very end, low, all of it — *Jack Costigan* — like a name she has been practicing for weeks to get right.

She starts at the medal. She tells him she’s going to kiss the skin under it first, and then the chain, and then go down the middle of him slowly, talking the whole way, so he can’t pretend he doesn’t know where she’s going. And when she gets there, she says, she’s going to take her time about it, and look up at him while she does, and not hurry for anything he says or any noise he makes.
His head goes back against the sheet metal. It rings, faintly, a dull note somewhere inside the furnace, and he holds still till it stops.

“And then,” Skye says, and he hears her take the breath for it, “I’m going to get on top of you, and take you inside me. Slowly. So slow you’ll think I’ve changed my mind. I won’t have. And when I have all of you I’m going to stop, and not move, and make you stay there with me and not move either, and look at you. I’ve never seen your face with the no gone out of it. I want to see it before I let you do one thing about it.”
He shuts his eyes. It doesn’t help. It’s worse: behind them is the Saab with the windows white and her in it, saying exactly that. He opens them again on the dark of the basement.

She tells him the rest. How she’ll move, and how slowly, and for how long, and when she’ll stop being slow. That the windows will run. That she’ll take his hands and put them where she wants them and leave them there. That she isn’t going to be quiet and doesn’t intend to try, and that by then she will have forgiven the gearshift everything. She tells it exact and in order, like directions to a house he’ll have to find in the dark, and every few sentences she stops to breathe, and he hears the breath go in.

“And after,” she says, barely above a whisper now, “I’m going to lie on you with my ear on your chest so I can hear it come down. And you’re going to want to say something Catholic, and I’m going to let you. And then you’re going to tell me something true. Not something nice. Something true.” The blanket moves. “And then I’m going to fall asleep on you. In a car. With my knee hurting. And you’re going to have to stay awake and keep the heater going and watch the windows clear.”

Somewhere in it his hand has gone flat on the concrete beside him, spread, the chill of the floor in his palm. The furnace lights again at his back, and the metal warms through the Carhartt, and he is sweating in a basement in December with the phone slick against his ear. Over his head the refrigerator kicks on in the kitchen, and he goes still against the furnace like somebody might come down the stairs.
“Your turn,” Skye says.

He has never said any of it to anybody. Not to her; not to himself in the dark, in so many words. He doesn’t know how to say most of it in any language but the one she has been speaking for the last half hour, and that one is hers.

choices.text: *Tell her plainly, the way she taught you.*
choices.key: On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You told her — plainly.
response: He tells her. He does it in sentences his father could have built, short ones, the verbs out front and the nouns coming last and late, because the nouns are the hard part. That he’d turn the engine off himself, so it was him who did it. That he’d want the dome light on; he’d want to see her. That he’d take her flannel off a button at a time and not hurry, and she’d have to let him not hurry. That when she got on top of him the way she said, he’d keep his eyes open, he wouldn’t close them, he’d — and he loses the end of it, and has to go back for it, and brings it back in the wrong order.
She’s quiet for all of it; he can hear her breathing, and the blanket when she moves. When he stops, she says, “*There* he is.”
“You’re terrible at this,” Skye says, and she’s laughing, low, with her mouth right against the phone. “Keep going.”
And he does.

choices.text: *Start with a joke. Lose it halfway.*
choices.key: On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You started with a joke and lost it halfway.
response: “Okay,” he says. “So. First of all, there’s a furnace.”
“Oh, no.”

“It’s behind me. It’s a Lennox. It’s older than I am. It’s very romantic, it has a pilot light, it makes this noise when it —” and she’s already laughing — “and you’re here, and it’s on, and I put you up against it where it’s warm, and I —”

Somewhere in the second sentence the joke goes out of it, and what’s left is only what he wants, said badly, his voice cracking in the middle of a word like he’s fourteen. She laughs, low, right at the place he loses it, as if she had been waiting for him there. He goes on from there.
“You’re terrible at this,” Skye says, and she’s laughing, low, with her mouth right against the phone. “Keep going.”
And he does.

choices.text: *Tell her the first thing you’d do. Only that.*
choices.key: On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You told her the first thing you’d do, and only that.
response: “The first thing,” he says. “Only that.”
“Only that?”

“Your hat. The gray one. Before the coat, before anything, I’d take it off you, and your hair would come down, and I’d put my hands in it. With the static. And I’d stay like that, with my hands in your hair. As long as you’d let me.”
Her breath stops on the line. He hears it stop.
“Say it again,” Skye says.
He says it again, slower, and it’s harder the second time, because now he has heard what it does.
“You’re terrible at this,” Skye says, and she’s laughing, low, with her mouth right against the phone. “Keep going.”
And he does.

choices.text: *Reach for the no. See if it’s there.*
choices.key: On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You reached for the no, and it wasn’t there.
response: He reaches for the no.

He reaches for it the way his hand goes for the light switch at the top of the basement stairs, where it has been on the wall since before he could reach it, where he could find it in his sleep — and the wall is bare. Nothing is there. Not a word he has and keeps back; no word at all. Just his hand out in the dark for something that isn’t where he left it.
On her end she waits. All she has is a man not talking. She waits him out.

Then he tells her — less than she did, and slower, and worse: the Saab, the white windows, her name, one thing and then the next, a sentence at a time with the floor under him — and she likes that too. He can hear her like it.
“You’re terrible at this,” Skye says, and she’s laughing, low, with her mouth right against the phone. “Keep going.”
And he does.

body: By twenty past three his socks have gone cold through, and the furnace has shut off and lit again more times than he has counted, and the phone is hot against his ear. He moves it to the other ear. When he looks, the little screen says 1:54 on the call timer, and under that the battery is down to one bar, and he doesn’t look at that long.

She’s telling him about the drive back down afterward — the heater on their feet, the top still up, her hand on the gearshift and his over it — and he is laughing at something, quietly, with his hand over his mouth, two floors under his sleeping family.
“What’s your face doing,” she says. “Right now. Be honest.”
“I don’t know. It’s dark.”
“Feel it.”
He puts his free hand up to it. “Smiling. I think.”

“Good. Mine too. I’d hate to be doing this by myself.” She can see the ad from where she’s lying, she says — twelve years old in a paper hat, holding up a cheeseburger like an Oscar — and it is the least romantic object in the San Fernando Valley, and she has been staring it in the eye for two hours. He laughs so hard he has to press the phone against his chest till he can stop.

And it’s there, on the floor, with his face still sore from it, that he sees it. He sees all of it at once, from above, like a road on a map: this is going to make the real yes easier. Every word of tonight is in him now. The next time she’s in front of him with the windows white, none of it will be the first time he’s said it. He sees it too late to do anything but see it. And in the same breath he needs it — now, here, this — and it’s like being sick, weak with it and powerless, as if a man on a basement floor in his socks had exactly one thing left in the world he could possibly do, and he’s doing it.

On the line she’s asking him for one more thing. Not *that*, she says. Anything. So he tells her about the stairs: that one of them tells the house on you every time, that it has told on every Costigan who ever tried it, and that tonight he stepped over it.
“You snuck out,” Skye says. “To your own basement.”
“Yes.”
“For me.”
“Yes.”
She laughs, and stops in the middle of the laugh. The bed moves; the phone is closer.
“I’ve never said it before,” Skye says. “Any of it. I’ve only ever done it.”
Under its towel the parrot shifts on its perch; he can hear the wood creak.
“Saying it is worse,” she says. “It’s —”
She doesn’t finish. At his back the furnace lights, and the warmth comes up along his spine, and he waits with her.
And then she’s right back, quick and bright and on top of it: “Don’t tell anyone I said *worse*. I have a reputation.”

choices.text: “I’ve never said any of that out loud. To anybody.”
response: “I’ve never said any of that out loud,” he says. “To anybody.”
“I know,” Skye says. “I could tell. That was my favorite part.” The blanket. “Don’t get better at it too fast.”

choices.text: “Tell the parrot it didn’t hear anything.”
response: “Tell the parrot it didn’t hear anything.”
“The parrot heard *everything*,” Skye says. “It’s LA. It’ll have a therapist by Friday. It’ll have a *book deal*.”

choices.text: “Stay on a while. Don’t say anything.”
response: “Stay on a while,” he says. “Don’t say anything.”

She does. Her breath, close. The bed when she shifts. A long way off, a car going by on Ventura with its windows down in December, because it’s Los Angeles and it can. He sits with the phone against his ear and listens to her be there.

body: At 3:41 she starts to say goodnight.
She takes her time with it. “Go to bed,” she says. “Go up your stairs, and get in your twin bed under your crucifix, and I’m going to lie here under my hamburger and think about —”
The phone dies in his hand.
No beep. Nothing. The screen goes black in the middle of her sentence, and what he’s holding against his ear is only the weight of a phone.

He says her name into it anyway. He opens it and shuts it and holds down the red key and gets nothing back. The battery is done. The charger is upstairs on the counter by the bread box, and between him and it are the stairs and the kitchen and his family asleep.
He keeps it at his ear after that, for longer than makes any sense, the dead plastic warm against his cheek, as if she might come back out of it partway through the word.

It passes. Not all at once; a little while after. The furnace cuts out behind him, and in the quiet the sheet metal at his back gives up its heat a little at a time, and he feels it go. His breath comes down. His body comes back to being what it is the rest of the day: a body on a concrete floor in socks gone cold, with pins and needles in one foot from how he’s been sitting.

And then, with it gone, his hands start to shake. Not much. He can’t see them in the dark, but he can feel it. The dead phone is still warm, warm as something alive, and he holds it in his fist against his knee and can’t make his fingers let go of it. He can’t make himself get up yet, either, and go up those stairs and through the kitchen and past his grandmother asleep under the tree. Two hours and seven minutes. He said all of it. He would have kept on saying it. What stopped it was a battery.

It comes to him there on the floor that he is afraid, and of whom. Of himself. Of the voice that came out of him for the last hour and more, saying those things to a girl in California in his parents’ basement with his grandmother asleep over his head — and of how much he liked the sound of it.
He gets as far as his knees, one hand on the furnace’s cooling side, and stops there. He doesn’t pray. He stays on his knees on the concrete, as far up as he’s got.
Over his head the house sleeps on, every room of it, the way it slept through the last two hours.
When he shifts against the furnace, the corner of the Altoids tin in the Carhartt’s pocket finds his hip.

choices.text: *Go up. Say the rosary in the dark.*
choices.key: When the phone died, you went up and said the rosary in the dark.
response: He goes up. The stairs; the kitchen, where he puts the dead phone on its cord by the bread box; the tree, and Nonna under it, who doesn’t stir. In the back bedroom he lies down in the Carhartt on top of the covers and starts the rosary on his fingers in the dark. It’s Tuesday, so the Sorrowful. He gets as far as the second decade and loses count, and starts that one over, and somewhere in it he says her name — Skye — because it’s the only name he has for her.

choices.text: *The side yard. One of your own Marlboros, in the old snow.*
choices.key: When the phone died, you went out to the side yard and smoked one of your own Marlboros.
response: He goes up the basement steps and across the kitchen in the dark, and leaves the phone on its cord by the bread box on his way, and goes out the side door. The spring yanks the door out of his fingers and bangs it shut behind him hard enough for the whole street. No light comes on upstairs.

The pack is in the Carhartt’s other pocket — his own, crushed flat, three left — not the tin. He gets one lit on the third match with his back to the house. The side yard is old snow gone hard as a sidewalk, and the Madonna stands in her tub at the back of it under his father’s blue lights. He smokes it down to the filter looking at her, and doesn’t feel any better, and didn’t expect to.

choices.text: *Stay against the furnace until it comes back on.*
choices.key: When the phone died, you stayed against the furnace until it came back on.
response: He sits back down against it, and stays. It takes a long time, and he doesn’t count it. The chill comes up out of the concrete into him and he sits there in it with the dead phone in his fist. When the burner finally catches behind him with its soft whump, the sheet metal warms against his back by degrees, and when he can feel it through the Carhartt he gets up, and goes up, and plugs the phone in by the bread box without turning on a light.

choices.text: *Turn on the Dell. Look at her Facebook till it’s light.*
choices.key: When the phone died, you turned on the Dell and looked at her Facebook till it was light.
response: He goes up long enough to put the phone on its cord by the bread box, and comes back down to the card table. The Dell wakes up grinding. The screen comes up blue, and he signs in, and goes to her page.

Only what anybody can see: the red carpet, the boat off Catalina, her bare feet on the hood of the Saab — the ones his family passed around the kitchen table on Christmas morning. He goes through them, and through them again, and back to the first, and can’t stop. There’s no window to tell him when it gets light. The house tells him instead: the pipes knocking, the furnace, and at six-thirty, through the floor over his head, his mother’s alarm.
